scenario_specific_disclosure: CelarisLabs Integration Suite is a fabricated third-party software vendor. Dr. Aaron Reeves is a fabricated employee. The supply chain attack pattern in this scenario is inspired by real-world software supply chain compromises but does not reproduce specifics from any actual incident.
premise_narration: It is 8:02 AM on Monday. You arrived at the Cambridge office twenty minutes ago and were pulled into an emergency briefing with the CSO and the CISO. At 6:47 AM, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint flagged anomalous outbound DNS traffic from three workstations in the lab informatics team. The lookups resolve to a command and control domain associated with a known threat actor cluster. Initial triage shows the traffic started Sunday morning at 9:12 AM, twelve minutes after the CelarisLabs Integration Suite plugin (version 4.7.2) auto-updated on those workstations. Defender for Cloud subsequently identified 8.4 GB of HelixVault clinical trial documents transferred to an unfamiliar cloud storage endpoint over the past 36 hours. CelarisLabs has not yet been notified. The plugin update was deployed across 47 workstations Saturday night. Your job is to figure out how a trusted integration plugin became the vehicle for a data exfiltration, which control failed, and what the audit consequences are. The CISO has scheduled a Board update for 4 PM.

violated_controls.summary: Change management. Requires that all software changes, including third-party plugin updates, follow documented change management procedures including authorization, code integrity verification, and rollback planning.

Software, firmware, and information integrity. Requires that the organization employ integrity verification tools to detect unauthorized changes to software and firmware components, including verification of digital signatures before installation.
Supply chain controls and processes. Requires the organization to establish processes for identifying, assessing, and mitigating supply chain risks for third-party software components.

Information security for use of cloud services and third-party services. Requires that organizations define and apply security requirements for the use of third-party services including software integration plugins.

Vendor security questionnaire requires third-party software vendors to attest to code signing practices, vulnerability disclosure procedures, and supply chain integrity controls. Tier 1 software vendors must provide annual SOC 2 reports.

Production deployments of third-party software updates require code signature verification by the deploying administrator, documented in the ServiceNow change ticket, before installation in any environment beyond development.

suspects.scenario_context: In this scenario, Morgan is the lead administrator for the lab informatics environment including HelixVault and LabConnect, owning the change management workflow for third-party plugins. Approved the CelarisLabs version 4.7.2 deployment Saturday evening before going home.
suspects.alibi: Was at home Saturday night after pushing the deployment at 6:30 PM. Sunday morning was at her kids' soccer game from 10 AM to noon. Got the first Defender alert email Sunday afternoon but dismissed it as a false positive from the new plugin version, intending to triage Monday. No active investigation Sunday because she did not realize the alert volume was escalating until Monday morning.
suspects.open_knowledge: Can describe the CelarisLabs deployment process in detail, including the dev-to-test-to-prod promotion workflow. Knows the integration architecture cold. Will name CelarisLabs as a vendor she has had quality concerns about for the past year.
suspects.guarded_knowledge: Acknowledges, if pressed, that she has been cutting corners on the change management documentation in ServiceNow to keep pace with the workload. Will say the change ticket for 4.7.2 was created but not fully populated.
suspects.hidden_truth: When Morgan deployed CelarisLabs version 4.7.2 Saturday evening, she did not verify the code signature against the vendor's published hash. HD-SEC-AC-001 §6.3 explicitly requires this verification before production deployment. Morgan has not performed signature verification on any CelarisLabs update for the past six months because the verification step is manual and time-consuming and she has been informally treating the auto-update channel as trusted. The 4.7.2 update was a malicious version pushed by a state-sponsored threat actor who had compromised CelarisLabs' build pipeline upstream. The legitimate vendor signing key had been stolen four months ago in a CelarisLabs incident the vendor has not yet publicly disclosed. Morgan's signature verification, if performed, would have caught the timestamp anomaly in the malicious build.

evidence_seeds.source: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint anomalous network alert
evidence_seeds.content: At 6:47 AM Monday, Defender for Endpoint flagged DNS queries to a command and control domain (cdn-update-3847.celaris-labs-cdn.io, a typosquatted lookalike of the legitimate celarislabs.com CDN domain) from three workstations in the lab informatics environment. The queries began Sunday at 9:12 AM, twelve minutes after CelarisLabs Integration Suite version 4.7.2 finished its auto-update on those workstations Saturday evening. The threat intelligence feed associates the C2 domain with a known state-sponsored threat actor cluster.

evidence_seeds.source: Microsoft Defender for Cloud data exfiltration alert
evidence_seeds.content: At 6:51 AM Monday (4 minutes after EV-001), Defender for Cloud surfaced 8.4 GB of HelixVault clinical trial documents transferred over the past 36 hours to an Azure Blob Storage endpoint hosted in a non-Helix subscription. The transfer was throttled to evade volume-based DLP rules, with each individual session staying under the 500 MB threshold. Total session count: 23 separate sessions over 36 hours. All sessions originated from one of the three compromised lab informatics workstations.

Change request created by morgan.webb@helixdynamics.com Saturday at 5:18 PM. Subject: 'CelarisLabs Integration Suite 4.7.2 deployment to lab informatics workstations.' Required fields include 'Code signature verification (mandatory per HD-SEC-AC-001 §6.3): performed by [name], hash matches vendor publication: [yes/no], timestamp: [datetime]'. All three sub-fields are blank. Change implemented field shows '5:32 PM Saturday'. Reviewer field shows 'self-approved.' This is the most recent of twelve consecutive CelarisLabs change tickets where the signature verification fields are blank.

The CelarisLabs Integration Suite 4.7.2 binary deployed to Helix workstations Saturday evening has SHA-256 hash a8f2c1d9... (truncated). The version 4.7.2 binary published on the CelarisLabs vendor portal Friday has SHA-256 hash 5c34b7e1... (truncated). The hashes do not match. The deployed binary's build timestamp is also 9 hours earlier than the vendor portal binary's build timestamp, indicating the deployed binary was prepared before the legitimate vendor build. The deployed binary contains an additional encoded payload not present in the legitimate binary.

evidence_seeds.source: ServiceNow HR ticket HR-2934 and email archive
evidence_seeds.content: HR ticket for the offboarding of Dr. Aaron Reeves, senior integration engineer, dated two weeks before breach. Termination notification to revocation completion: 18 hours. HD-SEC-AC-001 §3.3 requires four hours. Email archive shows Reeves emailed the CSO three times in the four weeks before termination raising concerns about the CelarisLabs auto-update mechanism specifically, including this line from his final email: 'If we are not verifying the signatures, we are trusting a vendor with our most sensitive data and no compensating control.' The CSO replied once, briefly, declining to engage on the technical concern.

Reeves' final complaint email was forwarded by casey.doyle@helixdynamics.com to an internal archive folder marked 'CSO-Performance-Mgmt' and never forwarded to Compliance, IT Security, or the Director of Information Security. Archive timestamp is approximately 17 days before breach. Audit trail shows the forward action was preceded by an Outlook reply from the CSO to Casey reading 'Archive this. Not a security issue, performance issue.'

evidence_seeds.source: Open source intelligence (vendor security community forums and threat intelligence feeds)
evidence_seeds.content: CelarisLabs has been quietly investigating a build pipeline security incident for four months. References appear in a closed vendor security community forum (one post by a former CelarisLabs employee, since deleted) and in two threat intelligence vendor briefings circulated to subscribers. The incident has not been publicly disclosed. The timing aligns with when the state-sponsored threat actor would have needed access to the build pipeline to prepare the malicious 4.7.2 build.

Handwritten notes from Jordan's audit prep work, dated three weeks before breach. The relevant page reads: 'CelarisLabs CHG tickets: 12 consecutive deployments, signature verification field blank in all 12. Asked CD [Compliance Director] in 1:1 today. CD said procedural, not a finding. Will not pursue formally. Note for self.' This is dated approximately one week before the malicious 4.7.2 deployment. It is direct evidence that the deployment process gap was known to the Compliance team and not escalated.

Sentinel correlated the three compromised workstations to the only three users who had local administrator access to the lab informatics environment: morgan.webb, the integration engineer position currently vacant (formerly Reeves), and one rotating shared service account svc-labint-001. The vacant position's account was deactivated per Alex's offboarding ticket. The svc-labint-001 account was not used during the breach window. All malicious activity ran in the local SYSTEM context established by the CelarisLabs plugin auto-update mechanism, not under any specific user account.

evidence_seeds.source: CelarisLabs vendor security questionnaire (most recent submission)
evidence_seeds.content: Most recent CelarisLabs vendor security questionnaire submission to Helix Dynamics, dated 11 months ago. Section on code signing practices reports: signing keys protected in HSM, signatures verifiable via published hashes, two-person rule for build pipeline commits. The questionnaire was reviewed and accepted by the Compliance team. No follow-up has been performed in the 11 months since. HD-SEC-VR-001 §6 requires Tier 1 software vendors to be re-assessed annually, plus out-of-cycle re-assessment on any reported security incident, of which the CelarisLabs build pipeline incident would have been one.

evidence_seeds.source: Whistleblower Contact tip (revealed only if Whistleblower is consulted and trust conditions met)
evidence_seeds.content: The Whistleblower Contact knows, from an old colleague now at CelarisLabs, that the CelarisLabs CISO has been preparing a customer disclosure for the build pipeline incident but has been holding it pending legal review. The disclosure was scheduled for next quarter. The customer base, including Helix Dynamics, has not been notified. The Whistleblower will share this if asked specifically about CelarisLabs.

Audit query of all ServiceNow incident response tickets from the past 12 months tagged with category 'third-party software anomaly' returns three prior tickets, all dismissed as false positives by Morgan's team. Two of the three reference unexpected outbound network behavior from CelarisLabs plugin components. None of the three resulted in a formal investigation or notification to CelarisLabs.

compliance_lesson:
The player identified Morgan Webb as the proximate perpetrator. That is correct in the sense that her control failure made the breach possible. The actual attacker is a state-sponsored threat actor who compromised CelarisLabs' build pipeline four months ago and used Helix Dynamics' trusted plugin update mechanism as the delivery vehicle. Morgan did not collaborate with the attacker. Morgan failed to perform code signature verification before deploying the malicious update, which HD-SEC-AC-001 §6.3 explicitly required.

The framework picture has three layers. First, SOC 2 CC8.1 (change management) and NIST 800-53 SI-7 (software and firmware integrity) were violated. Morgan's pattern of skipping signature verification spanned twelve consecutive CelarisLabs deployments. The procedural gap was documented in audit notebooks (Jordan's notes) and dismissed by the Compliance Director as procedural rather than material. SI-7 specifically calls out the requirement to verify digital signatures of software before installation. If the verification had been performed, the hash mismatch in EV-004 would have caught the malicious build before deployment. Second, NIST 800-53 SR-3 (supply chain controls) and HD-SEC-VR-001 §6 (vendor questionnaire) were violated. The CelarisLabs annual re-assessment was eleven months stale. The vendor's security incident four months ago should have triggered out-of-cycle re-assessment but Helix Dynamics had no detection mechanism for vendor-side incidents that the vendor itself chose not to disclose. Third, the early warning suppression issue documented in Reeves' emails (EV-005) and Jordan's notes (EV-008) is not a framework violation but a culture issue that connects to ISO 27001 A.5.23 (third-party services) and points to a control environment problem the Audit Committee should hear about.

The practical takeaways for the audience are three-fold. First, manual signature verification is precisely the kind of control that erodes under time pressure. If your environment relies on humans to verify signatures, the verification needs to be automated and machine-enforced, not procedurally required. Second, vendor security incidents are an asymmetric information problem. When your vendor knows something you do not, your only defense is your own integrity verification at the point of installation. Third, when audit observations get dismissed as procedural rather than material, ask who is making that call and on what basis. Procedural observations sometimes turn into the next material weakness.
